query: Many physical and chemical fabrication approaches have produced multi-element, near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles, yet their synthesis–structure–property relationships remain poorly established. This limits evaluation of their suitability for catalytic operation at 773–1173 K and thermoelectric use at 473–1923 K, including catalytic settings where low noble-metal content is desirable. What governs whether these nanoparticles preserve structural and chemical stability under such service regimes, and why? Formulate one testable mechanistic hypothesis, specify a controlled intervention that separates it from competing explanations, predict observations relative to a baseline, define its boundary conditions, connect it to the prior evidence summarized above, and provide a clear falsification test.

generation.hypothesis: High configurational entropy in near‐equiatomic multi‐element nanoparticles intrinsically leads to increased lattice distortion that raises atomic diffusion barriers, thereby kinetically suppressing phase separation and elemental segregation under high‐temperature service conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: Nanoparticles synthesized as single-phase, uniformly mixed high-entropy alloys (e.g., five or more elements in near-equiatomic ratios) via high-temperature processing, showing a well-dispersed, solid-solution structure.
generation.intervention: Prepare two sets of nanoparticles under otherwise identical conditions: one set using a high-entropy formulation (five or more elements) and a comparable binary (or low-entropy) alloy with a similar fraction of noble metals. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature annealing treatments.
generation.conditions: Anneal samples in an inert atmosphere at service-relevant temperatures (between 773 K and 1173 K) for defined durations (e.g., 30 minutes to 1 hour).
generation.structural_mediator: Degree of lattice distortion induced by multi-elemental mixing.
generation.mechanism: The mixing of many elements at nearly equal ratios increases the configurational entropy, which in turn induces substantial local lattice distortions. These distortions elevate diffusion barriers (or induce sluggish kinetics), significantly reducing atom mobility. As a result, even during prolonged high-temperature exposure, the nanoparticles retain their solid-solution structure without significant elemental segregation or phase separation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under identical high-temperature annealing, high-entropy nanoparticles will exhibit markedly lower atomic diffusion rates, minimal changes in particle size, and sustained uniform elemental distributions. In contrast, binary nanoparticles are expected to show higher diffusion coefficients, observable elemental segregation, and particle coarsening or phase separation.
generation.baseline: The behavior of binary (low-entropy) alloy nanoparticles under identical high-temperature conditions, which are predicted to undergo noticeable diffusion and segregation.
generation.boundary: This stabilization mechanism is expected to hold for nanoscale particles with near-equiatomic compositions fabricated via high-temperature methods. It may not fully manifest if other dominant effects—such as strong support-particle interactions or extreme temperature conditions beyond the 773–1173 K range—override the diffusion-slowing benefit of high configurational entropy.
generation.uncertainty: The exact quantitative increase in the diffusion barrier due to heightened lattice distortion and the minimal number of elements required to achieve effective stabilization remain to be precisely determined. Additionally, how support interactions may modulate this effect is not fully resolved.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize two groups of nanoparticles: one set as high-entropy (e.g., five-element near-equiatomic solid-solution nanoparticles) and a comparison set as a binary alloy with similar noble-metal content. Subject both sets to identical annealing treatments at multiple high temperatures (773 K, 873 K, and 1173 K) under an inert atmosphere. Use in situ transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) mapping to monitor changes in particle morphology, size distribution, and elemental homogeneity before and after annealing.
measurements: Quantitative determination of atomic diffusion coefficients via in situ TEM tracking or complementary molecular dynamics simulations.
EDX elemental distribution mapping pre- and post-annealing.
Phase analysis using X-ray diffraction (XRD) to check for any phase separation or segregation.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the high-entropy nanoparticles do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., reduced diffusivity, maintained uniform elemental distribution, and limited particle growth) compared to the binary nanoparticles under the same thermal conditions, or if both sets exhibit similar levels of segregation and phase separation, then the hypothesis that increased lattice distortion from high configurational entropy is the key factor in maintaining structural stability is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The dispersion stability of the MEA-NPs can be explained by the following two reasons. First, we used high temperatures for the MEA-NP synthesis, and as a result, they naturally have high thermal stability. Second, the defects of the carbon nanofibers help to anchor these MEA-NPs onto the substrate with improved thermal stability. In terms of the observed structural stability, we believe that it originates from the entropy stabilization effect. Thermodynamically, multi-elemental mixing increases the mixing of entropy and favors an alloy structure. Kinetically, the mixing among different elements also leads to increased lattice distortion (table S3 for Ru MEA-NPs) and, therefore, sluggish diffusion, which prevents phase separation and elemental segregation (, ). To further verify the structural stability, we performed MD simulations to calculate the self-diffusion coefficient of the Ru element in Ru-5 MEA and compared it with Ru in a binary Ru-Ni alloy. We also simulated the overall diffusion in the MEA-NP using a hybrid MC + MD simulation approach, in which the MC swaps were attempted at a constant frequency during the MD simulation to model the annealing conditions at 773 K. The entropy-stabilized structure has less atom diffusion due to high diffusion barriers and sluggish kinetics, resulting in uniform elemental distribution after annealing. Figure 4D shows the statistical probability of the nearest composition distributions for each element in Ru-5 MEA-NPs, displaying its microscopic/atomic arrangement of different elements. We found the nearest-neighbor sites of each element equal to its nominal composition with only short-range fluctuations. As a comparison, when it is fully diffusion equilibrated, clear elemental segregation, especially for Ru, Rh, and Ni, is observed (fig. S5A), indicating that the entropy-induced slow kinetics are the key to stabilize the structure for thermal annealing. Similar entropy-stabilization results were also found when there is an extension of MC + MD’s time scale to 50 ns (fig. S5B) and in the Ru-4 MEA-NPs (fig. S5, C and D). cited_evidence.text: The MD simulations indicates that the nanoparticles are quite stable on the edge planes of T-graphite even at extremely high temperatures. To further verify the thermal stability of such nanoparticles, we performed in situ TEM heating on the CNFs decorated with Pt nanoparticles that were synthesized through ex situ Joule heating method. The ex situ formed nanoparticles appear to have very similar morphology to the in situ observations reported in this work. As it can be seen in Fig. 7a, the ultra-fine nanoparticles are located at wrinkled edge planes showing FCC structure (inset of Fig. 7a). The Pt-decorated CNFs are evaluated at various temperatures (573 K, 773 K, 973 K, and 1173 K). As shown in the high angle annular dark field (HAADF)-STEM image in Fig. 7b, the ultra-small Pt nanoparticles are well dispersed on CNF at room temperature (RT). High temperatures are expected to be detrimental to the nanoclusters’ stability, since the nanoparticles would fuse into larger particles to reduce the surface energy at elevated temperatures.
